notes:
# Psalm 27: Research notes for a verse-by-verse commentary

**How these notes were gathered:** I read Enduring Word (Guzik), Spurgeon's *Treasury of David*, Matthew Henry, the Pulpit Commentary, the StudyLight and BibleHub verse pages (Barnes, Calvin, Gill, Clarke, Wesley, Benson, Ellicott), the NET Bible notes, bible.org, GotQuestions and Augustine on New Advent. I did not find anything on the chosen Lutheran, Pentecostal or Orthodox sites, or any prosperity or word-of-faith teaching on this psalm. Those categories are left out.

---

## Whole psalm

- **Two halves.** The first and second halves of the psalm are so different that many suggest it was two psalms stitched together. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-27/
- **The other side.** Coffman argues the psalm is one unit. He cites Yates: the same simple trust runs through the whole psalm, and this is the very same attitude encountered in the first six verses. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-8.html
- **Change of tone at v. 7.** The Pulpit Commentary says that from v. 7 the strain now entirely changes. The rhythm alters from a jubilant double beat to a slow and mournful cadence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **Setting.** The Pulpit Commentary places the psalm during Absalom's revolt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **A different setting.** The Greek Old Testament (Brenton's translation) titles it "A Psalm of David, before he was anointed." https://biblehub.com/psalms/27-1.htm

---

## v. 1: "The LORD is my light and my salvation"

**Traditional reading**
- **A unique title for God.** Guzik, quoting Boice, says this is the only direct application of the name *light* to God in the Old Testament. John uses the same idea of Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-27/
- **"Salvation."** Guzik takes this as rescue both now and for eternity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-27/
- **"Light" in Barnes.** God guides him. Darkness is the emblem of distress, trouble, perplexity, and sorrow; light is the emblem of the opposite of these. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-1.html
- **Borrowed light (Matthew Henry).** David's people called him the "light of Israel." Henry says David admits he shone as the moon does, with a borrows light. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-1.html
- **"Stronghold."** Ellicott prefers defence or bulwark; Heb., maôz. He also notes that Oxford University's motto, *Dominus illuminatio mea*, comes from this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/27-1.htm ; https://biblehub.com/psalms/27-1.htm

**Modern scholarship**
- The NET translates the verse "The Lord delivers and vindicates me!" Its note says "light" is often a picture of deliverance and the blessings it brings. Another option is that it means divine guidance (Ps 43:3). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27

**Catholic (Augustine)**
- Augustine reads the psalm as spoken by Christ's young soldier... on his coming to the faith. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm

## v. 2: "My enemies and foes stumbled and fell"

- **"Devour my flesh."** Barnes says this is not literal cannibalism. The comparison is one that is drawn from the fierceness of wild beasts rushing on their prey. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-2.html
- **They fell by themselves.** Matthew Henry notes the text does not say David struck them down. They were so confounded and weakened that they could not go on with their enterprise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_027.cfm
- **Past experience feeds faith.** Spurgeon calls the verse an instance of the way in which experience should be employed to reassure our faith in times of trial. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps027.cfm
- **Grammar (NET).** The Hebrew verbal forms are perfects. The NET reads the verse as a general statement, but it could also report a past event. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27
- **Augustine.** He makes the verse spiritual: mockers try to devour not me, but rather my fleshly desires. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm

## v. 3: "Though an army encamps around me"

- **Calvin.** "Armies" stands for whatever is most formidable in the world. God's power on David's side is far above theirs. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-3.html
- **Spurgeon.** The encamping host often inspires greater dread than the same host in actual affray. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps027.cfm
- **"In this I will be confident" (Pulpit).** This can mean either "because the Lord is my light" or "even if war comes." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **Augustine.** He applies the verse to the world persecuting the believer. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm

## v. 4: "One thing I have asked"

**Traditional reading**
- **Spurgeon on single-mindedness.** Divided aims tend to distraction, weakness, disappointment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps027.cfm
- **God, not the building.** Guzik says the tabernacle of David's day was a humble tent. What drew him was the beauty of the Lord that was to be found at the temple in a special way (Boice). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-27/
- **Pulpit.** David seems to be barred from the sanctuary and feels that as a terrible loss. "Beauty" means God's gracious attributes, not the outward look of the sanctuary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **Sibbes (in Spurgeon).** David saw the inward spiritual beauty of those spiritual things. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps027.cfm

**Modern scholarship**
- The NET says "the Lord's house" probably means the tabernacle if David wrote the psalm, or else the temple. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27

**Catholic (Augustine)**
- To "dwell in the house" means staying among them who hold the unity and the truth of the Lord's faith throughout the world. This points toward a final vision of God face to face. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm

## v. 5: "He will hide me in His shelter… set me high upon a rock"

**Traditional reading**
- **Not literal (Pulpit).** This is not to be understood literally. David means that his spirit will find a refuge with God in times of trouble. It does not mean he will physically hide in the tabernacle, as some Jewish expositors argue. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **Sanctuary custom.** Poole (in Spurgeon) sees an allusion to offenders who fled to the altar for safety, as in 1 Kings 2:28. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps027.cfm
- **Not a promise of no trouble.** Guzik: God promises not... to prevent all trouble, but to give security and blessing even in the midst of it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-27/
- **The "rock."** The Pulpit says it is God himself. Gill reads it as Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-5.html
- **Calvin.** Even while cut off from the visible sanctuary, David is sure that wherever he may be, he shall experience the protecting power of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-5.html

**Modern scholarship**
- The NET says the three verbs in v. 5 look ahead to God's positive answer to the prayer in vv. 7–12. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27

**Catholic (Augustine)**
- The "tabernacle" is the dispensation of His Incarnate Word (God's saving work through Christ), in times of temptation. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm

## v. 6: "My head will be held high… sacrifices with shouts of joy"

- **Pulpit.** David confidently expects victory, return from exile and access to the sanctuary again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **Barnes on "head lifted up."** In affliction a person bows down his head; in prosperity he lifts it up. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-6.html
- **Calvin.** By making a vow of thanksgiving in advance, David confirms himself again in the hope of deliverance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-6.html
- **Spurgeon.** David arranged ahead of time what he would do after the victory, guided by gratitude. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps027.cfm
- **NET.** The Hebrew is "sacrifices of a shout for joy," meaning sacrifices offered with a joyful shout. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27

## v. 7: "Hear, O LORD, my voice"

- **Spurgeon.** The pendulum of spirituality swings from prayer to praise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps027.cfm
- **Barnes.** The prayer comes from a returning sense of danger. His earlier assurance led him to pray rather than stop him praying. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-7.html
- **Pulpit.** There is no "when" in the original. The clauses are short, and broken. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **Gill.** "Have mercy" includes both rescue from trouble and forgiveness of sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-7.html

## v. 8: "My heart said, 'Seek His face'"

**Traditional reading**
- **God calls first.** One older writer in Spurgeon's collection says God must seek us, before we can seek him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps027.cfm
- **Matthew Henry.** Coming to the King uninvited would be presumptuous. David answers God's invitation, like someone touching the "golden sceptre" held out to him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_027.cfm
- **Calvin.** He sees a mutual conversation between God and the prophet. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-8.html
- **Pulpit.** The command "Seek ye my face" goes back to David's own words when the ark was brought to Zion (1 Chr 16:11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm

**Disagreement among older commentators**
- **Delitzsch** (on the BibleHub page) says There is no retrospective reference to any particular passage of the Law. The prayer rests on God's commands and promises in general. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/27-8.htm

**Modern scholarship: a hard Hebrew text**
- **NET.** In the Hebrew, "seek" is plural, which does not fit. The NET changes the reading to "his face" and translates "My heart tells me to pray to you." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27
- **Clarke.** He suspected a copying error. He rejects one proposed fix as too drastic because it is supported by neither MSS. nor *Versions*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-8.html
- **bible.org.** The words "When You said" in some translations are added (italics in NASB/NKJV). The verse is best read as a dialogue in which One calls and the other appropriately responds. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21513

**Catholic (Augustine)**
- Augustine follows the Latin "I have sought your countenance." He seeks God himself, not any reward apart from God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm

## v. 9: "Hide not Your face from me"

- **Pulpit.** David and other believers sometimes felt God's face was hidden. The commentary suggests God usually sends that feeling as discipline, to turn the heart back to him. It adds that God's past goodness is our chief ground of confidence for the future. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **Guzik.** David uses God's past help as a reason to ask for, and expect, future help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-27/
- **Matthew Henry.** David admits he deserves God's displeasure but begs not to be cast off: for what is hell but that? https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_027.cfm
- **NET.** "Hide the face" can mean "ignore," or more strongly "reject." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27

## v. 10: "Though my father and mother forsake me"

- **Pulpit.** We are not to gather from this that David's father and mother had forsaken him. They were probably dead at the time of his flight from Absalom. What David means is that, even if forsaken by his nearest and dearest, he would not be forsaken by God. The expression is proverbial. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **Matthew Henry.** God takes him up as a lost sheep is taken up. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-7.html
- **NET.** The Hebrew can be translated as a real past event ("though my father and mother have abandoned me"). "Receive" literally means "gather me in." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27
- **Augustine.** "Father and mother" are the kingdom and city of this world, which abandon the person who seeks God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm

## v. 11: "Teach me Your way… a level path"

**Traditional reading**
- **Spurgeon.** David does not ask to have his own way. The prayer shows an humble sense of personal ignorance, great teachableness of spirit, and cheerful obedience of heart. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps027.cfm
- **Matthew Henry.** He asks to understand God's providences and to know his duty in doubtful cases. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_027.cfm

**A difference among older commentators**
- **Calvin.** He mentions a common view that David is asking the Spirit to keep him from matching his enemies' violence. He says this is useful teaching but does not seem to agree with the scope of the passage. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-11.html
- **Barnes.** The word for "enemies" comes from a verb meaning "to twist," and so "to oppress." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-11.html

**Modern scholarship**
- **NET.** The "level path" is God's moral principles, which will keep the psalmist blameless before his accusers. The enemies are literally "those who watch me." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27

## v. 12: "False witnesses… breathing out violence"

- **Pulpit.** "The will of my foes" is literally their "soul," meaning their desire. It links the false witnesses to Absalom's party, which accused David of cruelty to Saul's house (2 Sam 16:8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **NET: a different reading.** The word traditionally translated "breathe out" is better taken as a noun meaning "witness." That gives "a testifier of violence." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27
- **Augustine.** The false witnesses are those who try to call the believer back from God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm

## v. 13: "I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living"

**An unfinished sentence**
- **Pulpit.** The Hebrew deliberately breaks off (a figure of speech called aposiopesis): "had I not believed…, then…". David shrinks from stating the consequences. https://biblehub.com/psalms/27-13.htm
- **NET.** It supplies "Where would I be…" to make the meaning clear. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27
- **Clarke.** He thinks the added words "I had fainted" weaken the sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-13.html
- **Barnes.** He thinks the added words undoubtedly express the true sense of the passage. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/psalms/27-13.html
- **Gill.** He notes that the Hebrew word for "unless" is one of fifteen words marked with special dots in the Hebrew Bible. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/psalms/27-13.html

**Where is "the land of the living"? (a real difference)**
- **This life.** The Pulpit says it means this present world. GotQuestions says David believed that God would hear his cries and answer his prayer before he died. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm ; https://www.gotquestions.org/land-of-the-living.html
- **Several meanings at once.** Matthew Henry allows this world, Canaan, or heaven: It is that alone that may truly be called *the land of the living,* where there is no more death. This earth is the land of the dying. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-13.html
- **Both lives (Guzik).** God would show his goodness in this life (as well as the next). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-27/
- **Methodist (Wesley).** David wanted this mercy in this life not because he placed his portion in these things; but because the truth and glory of God, were highly concerned in making good the promise of the kingdom to him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-13.html
- **Gill (Baptist).** He includes both God's providential care and all spiritual blessings in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/27-13.html
- **Spurgeon (Baptist).** We must believe to see, not see to believe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/27-13.htm
- **Note:** these are differences of emphasis between individual writers. I did not find sources showing that whole denominations split over this verse.

**Present-life blessing (closest material to modern "blessing" teaching)**
- A BibleHub study note says the verse points to God's present intervention. It adds that God's promises often include both spiritual and material well-being for His people, and that the phrase also connects to the hope of resurrection. https://biblehub.com/study/psalms/27-13.htm
- I found no source discussing a prosperity or word-of-faith reading of this verse.

**Catholic (Augustine)**
- "The land of the living" is the place where there is no place for falsity, which is heavenly. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm

## v. 14: "Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous"

**Who is being spoken to? (a difference)**
- **To himself (Pulpit).** This is an exhortation, not to others, but to himself. His stronger self is urging his weaker self to wait on the Lord's timing. Make an effort to be strong, and God supplies the strength. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/27.htm
- **To others.** Guzik heads this verse "An encouragement to others." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-27/

**What "waiting" means**
- **Not passive (Guzik).** Waiting on the Lord is not a passive sitting around until the LORD does something. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-27/
- **Hebrew word.** BibleHub notes that the verb (*qavah*) conveys an active, expectant waiting, rooted in trust in God's timing and faithfulness. https://biblehub.com/psalms/27.htm
- **NET.** It translates "Rely on the Lord!" with "wait" as an alternative. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Psa&chapter=27

**Catholic (Augustine)**
- Waiting is arduous for a mortal, it is slow to a lover. Don't assume that what you haven't yet received has been refused. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm
